---
title: "Regression as a sequence of extensions"
---

A regression model describes how a response distribution changes with predictors. We will not introduce the full architecture at once.

The linear-regression sequence begins with one question: how does a conditional mean change with one numerical predictor? We then add a response distribution, fit the line, quantify coefficient uncertainty, calculate residuals, and check whether the fitted model reproduces relevant patterns. Multiple predictors appear only after every part of the one-predictor model is in place.

Generalized linear models retain this regression structure for responses whose support is not the real line. We introduce the link-function architecture before treating binary responses, counts, and bounded responses separately.

Mixed-effects models address another problem: repeated speakers, items, verbs, documents, or languages. We first identify the repeated units and the desired generalization, then add random intercepts, random slopes, and nonnormal response families one step at a time.

The pages use distinct linguistic examples where possible. A dataset appears again only when several pages are successive steps of one analysis, such as inspecting a response, fitting its model, and checking its predictions.

Begin with [conditional means](regression-models.qmd). After the linear sequence, follow the separate [generalized linear model](why-generalized-linear-models.qmd) and [structured data](structured-data.qmd) branches shown on the [chapter dependency graph](../learning-path.qmd).
